latin:
Arma virumque canō, Trōiae quī prīmus ab ōrīs
Ītaliam, fātō profugus, Lāvīniaque vēnit
lītora, multum ille et terrīs iactātus et altō
vī superum saevae memorem Iūnōnis ob īram;
multa quoque et bellō passus, dum conderet urbem,
inferretque deōs Latiō, genus unde Latīnum,
Albānīque patrēs, atque altae moenia Rōmae.
modelTranslation: I sing of arms and the man who first came from the shores of Troy to Italy and the Lavinian shores, an exile by fate, he much buffeted both on the lands and on the deep by the violence of the gods above, on account of the unforgetting anger of savage Juno; having suffered much in war also, until he might found a city and bring his gods into Latium — from which came the Latin race, the Alban fathers, and the walls of lofty Rome.
notes: The proem is one long periodic sentence. The commonest failure is to translate it as a list of independent clauses instead of tracking qui … venit as the spine.

segments.literal: I sing of arms and the man
segments.requirement: Present tense of canō; both accusative objects rendered.
pitfalls: "Arms and the man I sing" is fine; "I sang" is not — canō is present.

segments.literal: who first from the shores of Troy
segments.requirement: Trōiae as genitive with ōrīs; prīmus as a nominative adjective agreeing with quī.
pitfalls: Rendering prīmus adverbially as "at first" rather than "first (to do it)".

segments.requirement: Accusative of place to which, without a preposition (poetic).
pitfalls: Treating Ītaliam as the direct object of vēnit.

segments.literal: an exile by fate / a fugitive because of fate
segments.requirement: fātō as ablative (cause or means); profugus as a nominative adjective describing the man.

segments.literal: and came to the Lavinian shores
segments.requirement: Perfect vēnit; lītora accusative of place to which; Lāvīnia agreeing with lītora.
pitfalls: Making lītora the object of vēnit.

segments.literal: he, much buffeted both on the lands
segments.requirement: iactātus as a perfect passive participle agreeing with ille; multum adverbial.
pitfalls: Translating iactātus as a finite verb ("he was tossed") — it is a participle here.
Missing that et … et means "both … and".

segments.requirement: altō as a substantive ablative, "the deep (sea)".
pitfalls: Reading altō as an adjective with no noun to modify.

segments.literal: by the violence of the gods above
segments.requirement: vī ablative of means/cause; superum as a syncopated genitive plural (= superōrum).
pitfalls: Missing that vī is from vīs.

segments.literal: on account of the unforgetting anger of savage Juno
segments.requirement: ob + accusative īram; memorem agreeing with īram; saevae with Iūnōnis.
pitfalls: Attaching memorem to Iūnōnis — it is accusative, agreeing with īram.

segments.literal: having also suffered many things in war as well
segments.requirement: passus as a deponent perfect participle, active in meaning, with multa as its object.
pitfalls: Translating passus passively ("having been suffered") — patior is deponent.
Missing multa as a neuter plural object.

segments.literal: until he might found a city
segments.requirement: dum + imperfect subjunctive expressing anticipation, not simple time.
pitfalls: "while he was founding" — the subjunctive marks purpose/anticipation, so "until he could found".

segments.literal: and might bring his gods into Latium
segments.requirement: Second verb of the dum clause, still subjunctive; Latiō as dative or locatival ablative.
unde as a relative adverb; the verb is understood.
Nominative plural continuing the same understood verb.
pitfalls: Changing case: patrēs here is nominative, not accusative.

segments.literal: and the walls of lofty Rome
segments.requirement: altae as genitive agreeing with Rōmae, not with moenia.
pitfalls: Attaching altae to moenia ("high walls") — moenia is neuter plural, altae is genitive singular.

latin:
excudent alii spirantia mollius aera
(credo equidem), vivos ducent de marmore vultus,
orabunt causas melius, caelique meatus
describent radio et surgentia sidera dicent:
tu regere imperio populos, Romane, memento
(hae tibi erunt artes), pacique imponere morem,
parcere subiectis et debellare superbos.
modelTranslation: Others will hammer out breathing bronzes more softly (I for my part believe it), they will draw living faces out of marble, they will plead cases better, and they will trace the movements of the sky with the rod and tell of the rising stars: you, Roman, remember to rule the peoples with your power — these will be your arts — and to impose the custom upon peace, to spare the conquered and to war down the proud.
notes: The four infinitives after memento (regere, imponere, parcere, debellare) are the backbone of the passage. Losing any one of them costs a segment.

segments.requirement: Future tense; alii as the subject, "others (than you)".
pitfalls: Present "others hammer out" for the future.
Reading alii as "the others" in a way that loses the Greeks/Romans contrast.

segments.requirement: aera as neuter accusative plural; spirantia agreeing with it; mollius as a comparative adverb.
pitfalls: Taking mollius as an adjective with aera rather than an adverb with spirantia.

segments.requirement: First person present; equidem as an emphasising particle.

segments.literal: they will draw living faces out of marble
segments.requirement: Future ducent; de + ablative; vivos agreeing with vultus.
pitfalls: "lead" for ducent — here it is "draw out, mould".

segments.requirement: Future; causas as the object; melius comparative adverb.
pitfalls: "pray" for orabunt — with causas it is the legal sense, "plead".

segments.literal: and will trace the movements of the sky with the rod
segments.requirement: caeli genitive; radio ablative of means.
pitfalls: Missing that meatus is accusative plural (fourth declension).

segments.literal: and will tell of the rising stars
segments.requirement: surgentia as a present participle agreeing with sidera.
pitfalls: Turning surgentia into a finite verb.

segments.literal: you, to rule the peoples with power
segments.requirement: regere as an infinitive depending on memento; imperio ablative of means; emphatic tu.
pitfalls: Reading regere as a passive infinitive or as an imperative.

segments.requirement: Vocative singular.
pitfalls: Rendering as nominative "the Roman" — it is direct address.

segments.requirement: Future imperative of memini, governing the infinitives.
pitfalls: Missing that it governs all four infinitives.

segments.requirement: tibi as dative of possession or reference; future erunt.
pitfalls: "to you" left unidiomatic where "your" is meant.

segments.literal: and to impose the custom upon peace
segments.requirement: Second infinitive after memento; paci dative with the compound verb impono.
pitfalls: Reversing it to "impose peace upon custom".
Missing the dative with a compound verb.

segments.requirement: Third infinitive; subiectis dative plural (parco takes the dative), used substantively.
pitfalls: Missing that parco governs the dative.

segments.literal: and to war down / to subdue completely
segments.requirement: Fourth infinitive; the de- prefix carries "utterly".
pitfalls: Rendering simply as "to fight", losing the force of the prefix.

segments.requirement: Accusative plural adjective used as a substantive.
pitfalls: Leaving it as an adjective with no noun.

latin:
tandem pauca refert: 'ego te, quae plurima fando
enumerare vales, numquam, regina, negabo
promeritam, nec me meminisse pigebit Elissae
dum memor ipse mei, dum spiritus hos regit artus.
pro re pauca loquar. neque ego hanc abscondere furto
speravi (ne finge) fugam, nec coniugis umquam
praetendi taedas aut haec in foedera veni.
modelTranslation: At last he replies a few things: "I shall never deny, O queen, that you have deserved well (of me) in the very many things which you are able to recount in speaking, nor will it irk me to remember Elissa so long as I myself am mindful of myself, so long as breath governs these limbs. I shall say a few things on behalf of the matter. I did not hope to conceal this flight by stealth — do not imagine it — nor did I ever hold out a husband's torches or come into these compacts."
notes: The indirect statement te … promeritam (esse) is the hardest thing here: the participle is doing the work of a whole clause after negabo.

segments.literal: at last he replies a few things
segments.requirement: Present tense; pauca as a neuter plural object.
pitfalls: Rendering refert as "it matters" — that is a different verb.

segments.requirement: te as the accusative subject of the indirect statement completed by promeritam.
pitfalls: Reading te as the direct object of negabo ("I will deny you").

segments.requirement: Relative pronoun, neuter plural; plurima superlative.
pitfalls: Reading quae as feminine nominative referring to Dido.

segments.literal: you are able to recount in speaking
segments.requirement: fando as an ablative gerund; enumerare complementary infinitive with vales.
pitfalls: Missing that valeo + infinitive means "be able".

segments.literal: never, O queen, shall I deny
segments.requirement: Future negabo; regina vocative.
Perfect participle agreeing with te, completing the indirect statement with esse understood.
pitfalls: Failing to supply "that you have…" — the whole indirect statement hangs on this word.

segments.literal: nor will it irk me to remember Elissa
segments.requirement: Impersonal pigebit with me accusative; meminisse governing the genitive Elissae.
pitfalls: Making me the subject ("nor shall I be ashamed").
Missing that memini takes the genitive.

segments.literal: so long as I myself am mindful of myself
segments.requirement: Verb sum understood; memor governing the genitive mei; ipse intensive.

segments.literal: so long as breath governs these limbs
segments.requirement: dum + present indicative for a contemporaneous action; hos agreeing with artus.

segments.literal: I shall say a few things on behalf of the matter
segments.requirement: loquar future of a deponent; pro + ablative.

segments.literal: nor (did I hope) to conceal this by stealth
segments.requirement: hanc looks forward to fugam three words later; furto is an ablative of means.
pitfalls: Failing to connect hanc with fugam across the intervening words.
Reading furto as dative, or as "theft" rather than "by stealth".

segments.requirement: Perfect tense, governing the infinitive abscondere.
pitfalls: Present "I hope" for the perfect speravi.

segments.requirement: ne + present imperative as a poetic prohibition; fugam completes hanc from segment 11.
pitfalls: Rendering ne finge as a statement.

segments.literal: nor did I ever hold out a husband’s torches
segments.requirement: Perfect praetendi; coniugis genitive; taedas accusative plural.
pitfalls: Reading praetendi as a passive infinitive.
Missing the reference to the wedding torch ceremony.

segments.requirement: Perfect veni; in + accusative of motion; haec agreeing with foedera.
pitfalls: Reading in foedera as ablative "in these treaties".

latin: Erat Miseni classemque imperio praesens regebat. Nonum Kal. Septembres hora fere septima mater mea indicat ei apparere nubem inusitata et magnitudine et specie. Usus ille sole, mox frigida, gustaverat iacens studebatque; poscit soleas, ascendit locum ex quo maxime miraculum illud conspici poterat.
modelTranslation: He was at Misenum and was commanding the fleet in person with full authority. On the ninth day before the Kalends of September, at about the seventh hour, my mother points out to him that a cloud was appearing, unusual in both size and appearance. He, having taken a sunbath and then a cold bath, had eaten a snack lying down and was studying; he calls for his sandals and climbs to a place from which that marvel could best be seen.
notes: Watch the tense sequence: Pliny slides between imperfect (regebat, studebat), historic present (indicat, poscit, ascendit) and pluperfect (gustaverat). A literal translation must keep them distinct.

segments.requirement: Miseni as locative; imperfect erat.

segments.literal: and was commanding the fleet in person with authority
segments.requirement: praesens as a nominative participle/adjective with the subject; imperio ablative.
pitfalls: Losing the durative force of the imperfect.

segments.literal: on the ninth day before the Kalends of September (24 August)
segments.requirement: Accusative of time; recognition of the Roman dating formula.
pitfalls: Translating word-for-word as "the ninth Kalends" without understanding the inclusive counting.

segments.requirement: Ablative of time when; fere adverbial.

segments.literal: my mother points out to him
segments.requirement: Historic present indicat; ei dative indirect object.
pitfalls: Rendering as past when the Latin is present — acceptable in idiomatic English, but a literal translation should keep the present.

segments.requirement: Indirect statement after indicat: nubem accusative subject, apparere infinitive.
pitfalls: Reading nubem as the object of indicat ("points out a cloud") — the infinitive makes it indirect statement.

segments.literal: unusual in both size and appearance
segments.requirement: Ablatives of respect/description; et … et correlative; inusitata agreeing with both.

segments.literal: He, having made use of the sun
segments.requirement: usus as a deponent perfect participle (active in meaning) governing the ablative sole.
pitfalls: Missing that utor takes the ablative.

segments.requirement: frigida ablative, with aqua understood; still governed by usus.
pitfalls: Leaving frigida as a bare adjective.

segments.literal: had taken a snack lying down
segments.requirement: Pluperfect gustaverat; iacens present participle.
pitfalls: Rendering the pluperfect as a simple perfect.
Turning iacens into a finite verb.

segments.requirement: Imperfect, distinct from the preceding pluperfect.
pitfalls: Flattening it into the same tense as gustaverat.

segments.requirement: Historic present; soleas accusative plural.
locum accusative with a verb of motion.
pitfalls: Reading ascendit as perfect — the context is a run of historic presents.

segments.requirement: Relative pronoun with ex + ablative, referring to locum.
pitfalls: Reading quo as an interrogative or as dative.

segments.literal: that marvel could best be seen
segments.requirement: Passive infinitive conspici with poterat; maxime superlative adverb.
pitfalls: Missing that miraculum is the subject of the passive.

latin: Erat Athenis spatiosa et capax domus sed infamis et pestilens. Per silentium noctis sonus ferri, et si attenderes acrius, strepitus vinculorum longius primo, deinde e proximo reddebatur: mox apparebat idolon, senex macie et squalore confectus, promissa barba horrenti capillo; cruribus compedes, manibus catenas gerebat quatiebatque.
modelTranslation: There was at Athens a roomy and spacious house, but ill-famed and unhealthy. Through the silence of the night a sound of iron, and if you listened more keenly, a clanking of chains, was heard — at first further off, then from close at hand. Soon a phantom would appear: an old man worn out by emaciation and squalor, with a long beard and bristling hair; he wore fetters on his legs and chains on his hands, and kept shaking them.
notes: The imperfects here are iterative — this happened again and again, not once. English "would appear" or "used to appear" captures it; a simple past loses the point of the ghost story.

segments.requirement: Athenis as locative plural.
pitfalls: Reading Athenis as ablative of means or dative.

segments.requirement: Both adjectives agreeing with the feminine domus.
Third-declension adjectives still agreeing with domus.
pitfalls: Rendering pestilens as "pestilent" without conveying "unhealthy, accursed".

segments.literal: through the silence of the night
segments.requirement: per + accusative; noctis genitive.
pitfalls: Reading noctis as nominative or ablative.

segments.requirement: ferri as the genitive of ferrum, not the infinitive of fero.
pitfalls: Reading ferri as the passive infinitive "to be carried" — a classic trap.

segments.literal: and if you listened more keenly
segments.requirement: Imperfect subjunctive in a generalising second-person condition; acrius comparative adverb.
strepitus nominative fourth declension; vinculorum genitive plural.

segments.literal: at first further off, then from close at hand
segments.requirement: Comparative adverb longius; primo adverbial; e + ablative.
pitfalls: Losing the sense of the sound approaching.

segments.requirement: Imperfect passive, iterative in force.
Imperfect, iterative; idolon a Greek neuter noun as subject.
pitfalls: One-off "appeared" instead of the repeated action.

segments.literal: an old man worn out by emaciation and squalor
segments.requirement: confectus perfect passive participle with two ablatives of means.
Ablative of description/quality.
pitfalls: Reading it as an ablative absolute.

segments.requirement: Second ablative of description; horrenti a present participle.

segments.literal: fetters on his legs, chains on his hands
segments.requirement: cruribus and manibus as datives/ablatives of place; compedes and catenas accusative objects; chiastic arrangement.
pitfalls: Reversing which restraint goes with which limb.

segments.literal: he was wearing and kept shaking (them)
segments.requirement: Two imperfects sharing the objects above.

latin:
O terque quaterque beati,
quis ante ora patrum Troiae sub moenibus altis
contigit oppetere! O Danaum fortissime gentis
Tydide! Mene Iliacis occumbere campis
non potuisse, tuaque animam hanc effundere dextra,
saevus ubi Aeacidae telo iacet Hector, ubi ingens
Sarpedon, ubi tot Simois correpta sub undis
scuta virum galeasque et fortia corpora volvit?
modelTranslation: O three and four times blessed, you to whom it happened to die before the faces of your fathers beneath the high walls of Troy! O Tydides, bravest of the race of the Greeks! That I could not have fallen on the plains of Troy, and poured out this life of mine by your right hand — where fierce Hector lies by the weapon of the grandson of Aeacus, where huge Sarpedon lies, where the Simois rolls along under its waves so many shields and helmets of men, and strong bodies!
notes: Aeneas's first words in the poem: a storm-tossed hero wishing he had died gloriously at Troy instead. mene … non potuisse is an exclamatory infinitive construction — no finite verb at all, just an accusative subject and an infinitive expressing disbelief/regret.

segments.literal: O three and four times blessed
segments.requirement: beati as a vocative plural adjective; terque quaterque as a fixed intensifying pair.
pitfalls: Treating terque quaterque as a literal count rather than "many times over".

segments.literal: you to whom, before the faces of your fathers
segments.requirement: quis as dative plural (an archaic/poetic form of quibus), the antecedent of the vocative beati.
pitfalls: Reading quis as the interrogative "who?" rather than the relative/dative "to whom".

segments.literal: beneath the high walls of Troy
segments.requirement: Troiae genitive with moenibus; sub + ablative of place where.
contigit impersonal + complementary infinitive oppetere, with quis (dative) as the person affected.
pitfalls: Treating contigit as a personal verb with a stated subject.

segments.literal: O bravest of the race of the Greeks
segments.requirement: fortissime vocative superlative; Danaum a syncopated genitive plural (= Danaōrum) with gentis.
pitfalls: Missing the syncope and reading Danaum as accusative singular.

segments.requirement: A patronymic vocative addressing Diomedes.
pitfalls: Missing that a patronymic in -ides/-ide names someone by their father, not by their own name.

segments.literal: that I [could] not fall on the plains of Troy
segments.requirement: Mene = mē + -ne, accusative subject of the infinitive occumbere in an exclamatory infinitive clause.
pitfalls: Reading -ne as a real yes/no question rather than an exclamation of disbelief.

segments.requirement: A second infinitive parallel to occumbere, completing the exclamatory clause begun by Mene.
pitfalls: Supplying a finite verb instead of keeping the infinitive construction.

segments.literal: and to pour out this life of mine by your right hand
segments.requirement: A third parallel infinitive (effundere); dextra ablative of means/instrument.
pitfalls: Attaching tua to animam instead of dextra — word order is interlocked (hyperbaton).

segments.latin: saevus ubi Aeacidae telo iacet Hector
segments.literal: where fierce Hector lies by the weapon of the grandson of Aeacus
segments.requirement: ubi as a relative adverb of place; Aeacidae genitive (patronymic for Achilles) with telo ablative of means.
pitfalls: Missing that Aeacidae refers to Achilles, not to Hector himself.

segments.requirement: A second ubi clause with the verb iacet understood from the previous clause.
pitfalls: Failing to supply the understood verb.

segments.latin: ubi tot Simois correpta sub undis
segments.literal: where the Simois, having swept [them] up under its waves
segments.requirement: Simois as the subject (a river-god/river name); correpta a perfect passive participle modifying the objects in the next segment.
pitfalls: Making Simois agree with correpta — correpta is neuter plural, agreeing with scuta/corpora ahead, not with the masculine river-name Simois.

segments.requirement: virum a syncopated genitive plural (= virōrum) with both scuta and galeas.
A third object continuing the list governed by volvit.
pitfalls: Losing track of the verb this whole list depends on.

segments.requirement: The main verb governing scuta, galeas, and corpora — all objects of this single verb at the very end of the sentence.
pitfalls: Missing that the verb comes last and governs everything listed before it.

latin:
nunc media Aenean secum per moenia ducit
Sidoniasque ostentat opes urbemque paratam,
incipit effari mediaque in voce resistit;
nunc eadem labente die convivia quaerit,
Iliacosque iterum demens audire labores
exposcit pendetque iterum narrantis ab ore.
post ubi digressi, lumenque obscura vicissim
luna premit suadentque cadentia sidera somnos,
sola domo maeret vacua stratisque relictis
incubat.
modelTranslation: Now she leads Aeneas with her through the middle of the city walls and shows him her Sidonian wealth and the city she has prepared, and begins to speak and stops in the middle of her words; now, as the day fades, she seeks the same banquet again, and, mad, begs again to hear the Trojan sufferings, and hangs again on the lips of the one telling them. Afterward, when they have parted, and the dimming moon in turn sinks its light and the setting stars urge sleep, alone she grieves in the empty house and lies on the couch he has left.
notes: The passage moves from Dido's public display of her city to her private collapse into obsession — note how the towers-stop-rising image later in the passage makes her private disorder a public, political one.

segments.literal: now [she leads] Aeneas with her, through the middle
segments.requirement: Aenean a Greek-declension accusative singular (not Latin -um); secum = cum + sē.
pitfalls: Failing to recognise the Greek accusative ending -an.

segments.requirement: Present tense ducit; per + accusative moenia.
pitfalls: Switching to past tense — the whole passage is vivid historic present.

segments.literal: and shows [him] Sidonian wealth and the prepared city
segments.requirement: Two accusative objects (opes, urbem) of ostentat; paratam a perfect passive participle agreeing with urbem.
pitfalls: Missing that paratam modifies urbem, not opes.

segments.requirement: incipit + complementary infinitive effari (a deponent verb).
pitfalls: Missing that effari is deponent — active in meaning despite its passive-looking form.

segments.literal: and stops in the middle of [her] speech
segments.requirement: in + ablative voce; media agreeing with voce.
pitfalls: Reading media as modifying an unstated noun rather than voce.

segments.latin: nunc eadem labente die convivia quaerit
segments.literal: now, as the day slips away, she seeks the same banquets
segments.requirement: labente die an ablative absolute; eadem agreeing with convivia (neuter plural).
pitfalls: Treating eadem as feminine singular nominative rather than neuter plural accusative.

segments.literal: and, mad, [begs] again to hear the Trojan sufferings
segments.requirement: demens a nominative adjective describing Dido; labores the object of the infinitive audire.
pitfalls: Missing the hyperbaton separating Iliacos from labores.

segments.requirement: The main verb governing the infinitive audire from the previous segment.
pitfalls: Losing track of which verb governs audire.

segments.literal: and hangs again from the lips of the one telling [it]
segments.requirement: narrantis a genitive present participle used substantively ("of the one narrating"), with ore.
pitfalls: Treating narrantis as agreeing with ore rather than functioning as its own noun-equivalent.

segments.requirement: digressi a perfect deponent participle (from digredior) with an understood sunt/erant and an understood subject (the guests).
pitfalls: Reading digressi as passive in sense — digredior is deponent.

segments.literal: and the dimming moon in turn suppresses its light
segments.requirement: obscura agreeing with luna, not lumen; lumen as the accusative object of premit.
pitfalls: Attaching obscura to lumen instead of luna — another interlocked (hyperbaton) word order.

segments.literal: and the falling/setting stars urge sleep
segments.requirement: cadentia a present participle agreeing with sidera; somnos accusative object of suadent.
pitfalls: Reading somnos as nominative plural rather than accusative.

segments.literal: alone she grieves in the empty house
segments.requirement: domo ablative of place where (no preposition, poetic); vacua agreeing with domo.
pitfalls: Missing the ablative-without-preposition and supplying "of the house" instead.

segments.requirement: stratis ablative (place where, or accompanying incubat); relictis a perfect passive participle agreeing with it.
pitfalls: Treating this as a separate ablative absolute rather than a phrase completing incubat.

segments.requirement: The main verb of the whole final clause, governing both sola domo maeret vacua and stratisque relictis in sense.
pitfalls: Missing that this single verb, held back to the very end of the sentence, is what the whole build-up has been waiting for.

latin: Dubito, constantiam vocare an imprudentiam debeam — agebam enim duodevicensimum annum -: posco librum Titi Livi, et quasi per otium lego atque etiam ut coeperam excerpo. Ecce amicus avunculi qui nuper ad eum ex Hispania venerat, ut me et matrem sedentes, me vero etiam legentem videt, illius patientiam securitatem meam corripit. Nihilo segnius ego intentus in librum.
modelTranslation: I am uncertain whether I should call it steadiness or foolishness — for I was in my eighteenth year: I ask for a volume of Livy, and read as if at leisure, and even go on making extracts as I had begun. Look — a friend of my uncle's, who had recently come to him from Spain, when he sees me and my mother sitting there, and me even reading, rebukes her patience and my unconcern. I go on nonetheless, absorbed in my book.
notes: The seventeen-year-old Pliny's calm under the collapsing city is the letter's most celebrated detail — as much a piece of self-presentation to Tacitus's later readership as a report of fact.

segments.latin: Dubito, constantiam vocare an imprudentiam debeam
segments.literal: I am uncertain whether I should call it steadiness or foolishness
segments.requirement: An indirect question (utrum/an-type, here with an alone) after dubito, with debeam as the subjunctive verb.
pitfalls: Missing that this whole clause is an indirect question, not two separate statements.

segments.literal: for I was [living/passing] my eighteenth year
segments.requirement: ago + a year-number as a Roman idiom for stating one's age.
pitfalls: Translating agebam as a generic "I was doing" without the idiomatic sense of age.

segments.literal: I demand/ask for a book of Titus Livius
segments.requirement: Titi Livi as a genitive of the author's full name.
pitfalls: Treating Titi Livi as two separate objects rather than one genitive name.

segments.literal: and I read as if at leisure
segments.requirement: quasi + per otium as a set comparative phrase.
pitfalls: Reading quasi as introducing an unreal condition here rather than a comparison.

segments.literal: and even make excerpts as I had begun [to do]
segments.requirement: ut + pluperfect coeperam, "as/just as I had begun"; excerpo present tense.
pitfalls: Missing that ut here means "as", not "in order that".

segments.literal: Behold, a friend of my uncle
segments.requirement: ecce as an interjection drawing attention to what follows; avunculi genitive.
pitfalls: Treating ecce as part of the grammar of the sentence rather than an interjection.

segments.latin: qui nuper ad eum ex Hispania venerat
segments.literal: who had recently come to him from Spain
segments.requirement: A relative clause with pluperfect indicative venerat (simple fact, not characteristic).
pitfalls: Rendering venerat as simple past "came" rather than pluperfect "had come".

segments.literal: when/as [he sees] me and my mother sitting
segments.requirement: ut here temporal ("when"); sedentes a present participle agreeing with me et matrem.
pitfalls: Confusing this temporal ut with a purpose or result ut.

segments.literal: and indeed sees me even reading
segments.requirement: videt the main verb governing this whole ut-clause's participial constructions; legentem a present participle agreeing with me.
pitfalls: Missing that videt is the delayed main verb for the whole ut clause begun two segments earlier.

segments.requirement: illius genitive singular (referring to the mother), with patientiam as one of two accusative objects of corripit.
A second accusative object of corripit, parallel to illius patientiam.
pitfalls: Missing the parallel structure with the previous segment.

segments.requirement: The main verb governing both patientiam and securitatem as its objects.
pitfalls: Supplying two separate verbs instead of one verb with two objects.

segments.literal: none the less / no more slowly for that
segments.requirement: Nihilo an ablative of degree of difference with the comparative segnius.
pitfalls: Missing the ablative-of-degree-of-difference construction with a comparative adverb.

segments.requirement: intentus a perfect passive participle used adjectivally, agreeing with the understood subject ego.
pitfalls: Translating intentus as a finite verb rather than a descriptive participle.

segments.requirement: in + accusative with intentus, "intent upon" — a fixed idiom, not ordinary motion-into.
pitfalls: Treating in librum as literal motion "into the book".

latin: Sub dio rursus quamquam levium exesorumque pumicum casus metuebatur, quod tamen periculorum collatio elegit; et apud illum quidem ratio rationem, apud alios timorem timor vicit. Cervicalia capitibus imposita linteis constringunt; id munimentum adversus incidentia fuit.
modelTranslation: In the open air, on the other hand, the fall of pumice stones, light and porous though they were, was feared; yet a comparison of the dangers chose this. And with him, indeed, reason overcame reason; with the others, fear overcame fear. They tie pillows placed on their heads with linen cloths; this was their protection against the things falling.
notes: ratio rationem … timorem timor is the letter’s best-known chiasmus: for Pliny the Elder one reasoned choice outweighed another, for the rest one fear outweighed another. The single vicit at the end serves both halves.

segments.literal: in the open air, on the other hand
segments.requirement: sub dio as a fixed phrase, “under the sky”; rursus as “in turn, on the other hand”.
pitfalls: Translating rursus as “again”, which makes no sense here.

segments.literal: of pumice stones, although light and porous
segments.requirement: Genitives depending on casus; quamquam concessive with the adjectives.
pitfalls: Making levium and exesorum agree with casus instead of pumicum.

segments.requirement: casus nominative singular (fourth declension), subject of the imperfect passive.

segments.literal: which, however, a comparison of the dangers chose
segments.requirement: quod referring to staying in the open; collatio subject, periculorum its genitive.
apud + accusative, “in his case”.
pitfalls: “near him” — apud here means “in the mind of”.

segments.requirement: ratio nominative subject, rationem accusative object of the vicit to come.
Parallel to apud illum.
pitfalls: Dropping the contrast with apud illum.

segments.requirement: timor subject, timorem object, vicit perfect governing both halves.
pitfalls: Missing that the word order is reversed (chiasmus) and swapping subject and object.

segments.requirement: Neuter plural accusative, object of constringunt.
imposita perfect passive participle agreeing with cervicalia; capitibus dative with the compound verb.
pitfalls: Making imposita agree with an understood subject.

segments.requirement: Ablative of means.
pitfalls: “on the linens” — it is the means of tying.

segments.requirement: Present tense (historic present) with the people as subject.
id subject, munimentum predicate nominative.
incidentia present participle used as a neuter plural noun, object of adversus.
Perfect of sum.

latin: Audires ululatus feminarum, infantum quiritatus, clamores virorum; alii parentes alii liberos alii coniuges vocibus requirebant, vocibus noscitabant; hi suum casum, illi suorum miserabantur; erant qui metu mortis mortem precarentur
modelTranslation: You could have heard the wailing of women, the crying of infants, the shouting of men; some were looking for their parents, others for their children, others for their spouses by their voices, and recognizing them by their voices; some were lamenting their own fate, others the fate of their families; there were those who, from fear of death, prayed for death.
notes: Pliny turns the darkness into sound: three noun pairs without conjunctions, then alii … alii … alii and hi … illi, and the paradox metu mortis mortem. Audires is a past potential: the reader is put on the shore.

segments.requirement: Imperfect subjunctive as a past potential (“you would have heard”).
pitfalls: “you heard” — it is not a statement of fact.

segments.requirement: ululatus accusative plural (fourth declension), object of audires.
A second object, with the genitive first.
pitfalls: Missing that quiritatus is a noun.

segments.requirement: Third object in the series, no conjunction.
pitfalls: Adding “and” is fine; changing the case is not.

segments.requirement: alii … alii … alii as “some … others … others”, with requirebant to come.
liberos “children”, not “free men”.
Third member of the series.

segments.literal: were trying to find by their voices
segments.requirement: vocibus ablative of means; imperfect.
pitfalls: “with voices” attached to the wrong verb.

segments.requirement: noscitabant frequentative imperfect; vocibus repeated.
hi … illi as “some … others”; suum reflexive.

segments.literal: those [lamenting the fate] of their own people
segments.requirement: suorum a substantive genitive plural, “of their own (family)”.
Deponent imperfect, active in meaning, governing both casum and (casum) suorum.
erant qui introducing a relative clause of characteristic.
metu ablative of cause.
precarentur deponent, imperfect subjunctive in a clause of characteristic.

latin: Est libertus mihi non illitteratus. Cum hoc minor frater eodem lecto quiescebat. Is visus est sibi cernere quendam in toro residentem, admoventemque capiti suo cultros, atque etiam ex ipso vertice amputantem capillos.
modelTranslation: I have a freedman, not without education. With him his younger brother was sleeping in the same bed. He seemed to himself to see someone sitting on the couch, moving knives towards his head, and even cutting off hair from the very crown of his head.
notes: visus est sibi cernere, “he seemed to himself to see”: Pliny keeps the dream at arm’s length. Three participles, residentem, admoventem, amputantem, all describe quendam and build the scene step by step.

segments.requirement: est with a predicate noun, completed by mihi.
Dative of possession.
Litotes: a negative of the opposite.
pitfalls: Dropping the non or the il-.

segments.requirement: cum + ablative of hic.
minor comparative of parvus.
Ablative of place where without in.
Imperfect: the background to the event.
videor with a dative; sibi reflexive.
Complementary infinitive with visus est; quendam accusative of quidam.
pitfalls: Reading quendam as “a certain one” attached to cernere’s subject.

segments.requirement: Present participle agreeing with quendam.
pitfalls: Making the brother the one sitting.

segments.requirement: Second participle with quendam.
pitfalls: Treating it as a finite verb.

segments.requirement: capiti dative with the compound verb; suo refers to the sleeper; cultros the object.
Climax of the series.

segments.literal: from the very crown of his head
segments.requirement: ipso intensive with vertice.
Third participle with quendam; capillos object.

latin: Ipse perveni ad fontem purissimum, ex quo videtur aqua debere perduci, sicut initio temptatum erat, arcuato opere, ne tantum ad plana civitatis et humilia perveniat. Manent adhuc paucissimi arcus: possunt et erigi quidam lapide quadrato, qui ex superiore opere detractus est
modelTranslation: I myself went to a very pure spring, from which it seems the water ought to be brought, as had been attempted at the start, by an arched structure, so that it does not reach only the level and low-lying parts of the city. A very few arches still remain; some can also be raised with squared stone which was taken from the earlier work.
notes: Pliny writes like an engineer’s report: the source, the method (arcuato opere) and its reason (ne … perveniat), then the materials at hand. videtur aqua debere perduci is a personal videor: “the water seems to need bringing”, better “it seems the water should be brought”.

segments.requirement: ipse intensive with the first-person subject; perfect perveni.
Superlative of purus.
pitfalls: “the purest spring of all” is acceptable; “pure” alone loses the superlative.

segments.requirement: quo relative referring to fontem; videtur personal, its subject aqua.

segments.literal: that the water ought to be brought
segments.requirement: Nominative aqua with the infinitive after videtur; perduci present passive infinitive.

segments.literal: as had been attempted at the start
segments.requirement: Impersonal pluperfect passive; initio ablative of time.
Ablative of means.
pitfalls: “with arched work” attached to temptatum only.

segments.requirement: ne introducing a negative purpose clause; tantum “only”.
pitfalls: Reading ne tantum as “not so much”.

segments.literal: to the level and low-lying parts of the city
segments.requirement: plana and humilia neuter plural substantives; civitatis genitive.
Present subjunctive in the purpose clause.
manent present, adhuc “still”.
Superlative of paucus; arcus nominative plural (fourth declension).
quidam subject; erigi present passive infinitive with possunt.
Ablative of means.
qui refers to lapide; superiore “earlier”.
Perfect passive.

latin: Proximo anno, domine, gravissima valetudine usque ad periculum vitae vexatus iatralipten assumpsi; cuius sollicitudini et studio tuae tantum indulgentiae beneficio referre gratiam parem possum. Quare rogo des ei civitatem Romanam.
modelTranslation: Last year, my lord, when I was afflicted by a very serious illness, right up to the danger of my life, I took on a masseur-doctor; for his care and devotion I can return equal thanks only through the favor of your kindness. Therefore I ask you to give him Roman citizenship.
notes: cuius is a connecting relative (= et eius): start a new English sentence. rogo des, with ut left out, is the usual shape of Pliny’s requests to Trajan.

segments.requirement: Ablative of time when.
Vocative, Pliny’s address to the emperor.
Ablative with vexatus; superlative.

segments.literal: right up to danger of my life
segments.requirement: usque ad “all the way to”; vitae genitive.
Perfect passive participle agreeing with the subject of assumpsi.
pitfalls: Turning it into the main verb.

segments.requirement: Greek accusative in -en; perfect assumpsi.
pitfalls: Missing that iatralipten is the object.

segments.requirement: Connecting relative; datives with gratiam referre.

segments.literal: only through the favor of your kindness
segments.requirement: beneficio ablative of means; tantum “only”.
gratiam referre “to repay”; parem agrees with gratiam.
pitfalls: “to bring back an equal favor” too literally.

segments.requirement: Main verb of the sentence.
Connective.
Introduces the request.
Present subjunctive in an indirect command, ut left out.
Dative indirect object.
Direct object of des.

latin: Nunc vero me cum absentiae tum infirmitatis tuae ratio incerta et varia sollicitudine exterret. Vereor omnia, imaginor omnia, quaeque natura metuentium est, ea maxime mihi quae maxime abominor fingo. Quo impensius rogo, ut timori meo cottidie singulis vel etiam binis epistulis consulas.
modelTranslation: But now the thought both of your absence and of your illness terrifies me with an uncertain and changing anxiety. I fear everything, I imagine everything, and, as is the nature of those who are afraid, I picture to myself most of all the things I most dread. So all the more earnestly I ask you to relieve my fear every day with one letter or even two.
notes: cum … tum, “both … and especially”, joins the two causes of worry. Quo impensius is an ablative of degree of difference with a comparative adverb: “by so much the more earnestly”.

segments.requirement: vero adversative.
pitfalls: “now truly” is weak; “but now” marks the turn.

segments.requirement: Accusative object of exterret, put first.

segments.latin: cum absentiae tum infirmitatis tuae ratio
segments.literal: the thought both of your absence and of your illness
segments.requirement: cum … tum correlative; genitives with ratio.

segments.literal: with an uncertain and changing anxiety
segments.requirement: Ablative of means.
Present, main verb with ratio as subject.
Deponent, active in meaning.
Second deponent, parallel.

segments.literal: and, as is the nature of those who fear
segments.requirement: quae relative looking forward to the clause; metuentium substantive participle.
pitfalls: Taking quae as the object of fingo.

segments.literal: those things most of all for myself
segments.requirement: ea object of fingo; mihi dative of reference.
pitfalls: “to me” as indirect object of something else.

segments.requirement: Relative clause; deponent abominor.
pitfalls: “which I most abhor” is fine; passive is not.

segments.requirement: Main verb of the clause.

segments.literal: so all the more earnestly I ask
segments.requirement: quo ablative of degree of difference with impensius.
ut introducing an indirect command; timori dative with consulas.

segments.latin: cottidie singulis vel etiam binis epistulis
segments.literal: every day with one or even two letters
segments.requirement: Distributive numerals; ablative of means.
pitfalls: “with single or double letters” loses the per-day sense.

segments.requirement: consulo + dative “look after”; present subjunctive.

latin:
Primus ibi ante omnis magna comitante caterva
Laocoon ardens summa decurrit ab arce,
et procul 'o miseri, quae tanta insania, cives?
creditis avectos hostis? aut ulla putatis
dona carere dolis Danaum? sic notus Ulixes?
modelTranslation: There first, before all, with a great crowd accompanying him, Laocoön, blazing, runs down from the top of the citadel, and cries from afar: ‘O wretched citizens, what great madness is this? Do you believe the enemy have sailed away? Or do you think any gifts of the Greeks are free of tricks? Is this how you know Ulysses?’
notes: Vergil leaves out the verb of speaking after procul and the est in quae tanta insania: supply both. Danaum is the short genitive plural (= Danaorum) and goes with dona.

segments.requirement: primus nominative, agreeing with Laocoon.
omnis = omnes, accusative plural with ante.
Ablative absolute.
pitfalls: “with a great accompanying crowd” as means.

segments.requirement: Subject with a present participle.

segments.literal: runs down from the top of the citadel
segments.requirement: summa “top of”; historic present.
A verb of speaking is understood.
Vocative, with cives to come.
est understood; quae interrogative adjective.
Present, introducing indirect statement.

segments.literal: that the enemy have sailed away?
segments.requirement: Accusative + perfect participle with esse left out; hostis = hostes.
pitfalls: “the enemies carried away” as a noun phrase.

segments.literal: or do you think that any
segments.requirement: putatis introduces a second indirect statement; ulla with dona.
careo + ablative of separation.
Genitive plural (= Danaorum) with dona.
notus predicate adjective, est understood.
Nominative subject.

latin:
illa vel intactae segetis per summa volaret
gramina nec teneras cursu laesisset aristas,
vel mare per medium fluctu suspensa tumenti
ferret iter celeris nec tingeret aequore plantas.
modelTranslation: She would fly over the tops of the blades of an uncut crop and would not have bruised the tender ears with her running, or she would make her way through the middle of the sea, held up by the swelling wave, swift, and would not wet her soles in the water.
notes: Two potential subjunctives, volaret and ferret, each with a nec clause; laesisset, pluperfect, sharpens the first. celeris is nominative, agreeing with illa, not genitive.

segments.requirement: Subject of both halves.
vel … vel correlative; genitive with gramina.
Imperfect subjunctive, potential; summa with gramina.
The noun summa modifies, held to the next line.
pitfalls: Treating gramina as a separate object.

segments.requirement: teneras agrees with aristas.
Pluperfect subjunctive; cursu ablative of means.
Object of laesisset.
Second half of the correlative.
medium with mare: “the middle of the sea”.

segments.literal: held up by the swelling wave
segments.requirement: Ablative of means; suspensa agrees with illa.
pitfalls: “suspended by a swollen flood” as agent with a.

segments.requirement: iter ferre “to make one’s way”; potential subjunctive.
Nominative, agreeing with illa.
Imperfect subjunctive parallel to ferret.
Ablative of means or place.
Object of tingeret.

latin:
pulsus ob invidiam regno virisque superbas
Priverno antiqua Metabus cum excederet urbe,
infantem fugiens media inter proelia belli
sustulit exsilio comitem, matrisque vocavit
nomine Casmillae mutata parte Camillam.
modelTranslation: When Metabus, driven from his kingdom because of hatred and his arrogant power, was leaving the ancient city of Privernum, fleeing through the midst of the battles of war he took up his infant as a companion for his exile, and he called her Camilla, from her mother’s name Casmilla, with part of it changed.
notes: The cum clause is postponed: pulsus … Priverno antiqua Metabus cum excederet urbe. Begin the English with “When Metabus …”. matris … nomine Casmillae runs across the line end: “by the name of her mother, Casmilla”.

segments.requirement: Perfect passive participle agreeing with Metabus.
ob + accusative, cause.
Ablative of separation with pulsus.
viris = vires, accusative plural of vis, also with ob.
Ablative of place from which; antiqua with urbe.

segments.literal: when Metabus was leaving the city
segments.requirement: cum + imperfect subjunctive, circumstantial; urbe ablative.
Object of sustulit.
Present participle with Metabus.

segments.literal: through the midst of the battles of war
segments.requirement: media “the middle of”; belli genitive.
Perfect of tollo.

segments.literal: as a companion for his exile
segments.requirement: comitem predicate accusative; exsilio dative.

segments.literal: and he called [her] … of her mother
segments.requirement: vocavit with two accusatives (her, Camillam); matris with nomine.
Ablative of means; Casmillae in apposition to matris.
pitfalls: “by the name of Casmilla” losing the mother.

segments.requirement: Ablative absolute.
Predicate accusative with vocavit.
pitfalls: Making Camillam the direct object of sustulit.

latin:
ne vetus indigenas nomen mutare Latinos
neu Troas fieri iubeas Teucrosque vocari
aut vocem mutare viros aut vertere vestem.
sit Latium, sint Albani per saecula reges,
sit Romana potens Itala virtute propago:
occidit, occideritque sinas cum nomine Troia.'
modelTranslation: that you not order the native Latins to change their ancient name, nor to become Trojans and be called Teucrians, or the men to change their language or alter their dress. Let there be Latium, let there be Alban kings through the ages, let the Roman line be powerful in Italian valor: Troy has fallen, and let it be fallen, together with its name.
notes: This depends on obtestor in line 820: “I beg you … that you not order”. Juno’s terms end in three jussives, sit, sint, sit, and a fourth with sinas: occideritque sinas, “and allow it to have fallen”.

segments.requirement: ne introducing an indirect command after obtestor (line 820); vetus with nomen.
Latinos accusative subject of mutare, indigenas agreeing with it.
Troas Greek accusative plural, predicate with fieri.
Present subjunctive governing the infinitives.
Present passive infinitive with predicate accusative.

segments.literal: or the men to change their language
segments.requirement: viros subject accusative; vocem “speech, language”.
Parallel infinitive.
Jussive subjunctive.

segments.literal: let there be Alban kings through the ages
segments.requirement: Jussive; per saecula “for ages”.
Jussive; Romana with propago.
virtute ablative of respect or means; propago subject.
Perfect.

segments.literal: and allow that it have fallen
segments.requirement: sinas jussive; occiderit perfect subjunctive depending on it, ut left out.
cum + ablative.
Subject of occidit and occiderit.
pitfalls: Leaving the subject until the wrong clause.

latin:
'tune hinc spoliis indute meorum
eripiare mihi? Pallas te hoc vulnere, Pallas
immolat et poenam scelerato ex sanguine sumit.'
hoc dicens ferrum adverso sub pectore condit
fervidus; ast illi solvuntur frigore membra
vitaque cum gemitu fugit indignata sub umbras.
modelTranslation: ‘Are you, clothed in the spoils of my own, to be snatched from me here? Pallas, Pallas sacrifices you with this wound and exacts the penalty from your criminal blood.’ Saying this, he buries the sword in the chest before him, burning with rage; but Turnus’ limbs go slack with cold, and his life with a groan flees, resentful, to the shades below.
notes: The poem’s last sentence. eripiare is the short form of eripiaris, a deliberative subjunctive in an indignant question. illi is a dative of reference: “for him the limbs are loosened”, i.e. his limbs.

segments.requirement: tu + the question particle -ne; hinc “from here”.

segments.literal: clothed in the spoils of my own [people]
segments.requirement: indute vocative of the participle, with spoliis ablative; meorum substantive.
eripiare = eripiaris, present passive subjunctive, deliberative; mihi dative of separation.
Subject repeated; vulnere ablative of means.
Present; the victim is te.
Object of sumit.
poenam sumere “exact a penalty”; scelerato with sanguine.
pitfalls: “takes punishment out of the blood” too literal, or “criminal” with poenam.

segments.requirement: Present participle with Aeneas.

segments.literal: the sword in the chest that faces him
segments.requirement: adverso “turned toward him”; sub pectore with condit.
Present; condo “bury, plunge”.
Nominative with the subject, Aeneas.
illi dative of reference (possession).
Present passive; frigore ablative of means.

segments.literal: and his life with a groan flees
segments.requirement: cum + ablative of manner.
pitfalls: “and life flees with the groan” is fine; “when” for cum is not.

segments.requirement: indignata deponent participle with vita; sub + accusative of motion.
